controls.statement: Maintain current system-context, component, deployment, and end-to-end data-flow diagrams.
Mark trust boundaries, external interfaces, administrative interfaces, support interfaces, authentication points, authorization points, and encryption boundaries.
Mark where sensitive data is collected, transformed, stored, cached, logged, exported, backed up, transferred, and deleted.
Identify every stateful component, asynchronous boundary, queue, common dependency, shared failure domain, and control-plane dependency.
Identify single points of failure, circular dependencies, and hidden dependencies.
Record material architecture decisions, rejected alternatives, and tradeoffs.
Update diagrams after material changes and verify documentation against the deployed environment.
Include all actors, trust boundaries, entry points, data stores, external systems, and administrative paths.
Model identity spoofing, unauthorized modification, information disclosure, denial of service, repudiation, and privilege escalation.
Model business-logic abuse, insider threats, compromised administrators, dependency compromise, and build-system compromise.
Model tenant escape, scraping, spam, fraud, automation, economic abuse, backup attacks, and support-channel social engineering.
Convert identified threats into requirements, controls, and tests.
Revisit the threat model after material scope or design changes.
Performance objectives are defined for every critical journey.
Objectives use meaningful percentiles rather than averages alone.
Frontend and backend performance budgets are documented.
Public pages meet approved loading, interaction, visual-stability, rendering, and responsiveness targets.
API latency targets are defined by endpoint or journey.
Database-query latency, count, and volume are measured.
Excessive queries, repeated fetches, blocking operations, and unbounded responses are eliminated.
Payload sizes are bounded and compression is enabled appropriately.
Images, fonts, scripts, styles, media, and critical resources are delivered efficiently.
Noncritical work is deferred without harming accessibility, correctness, or user trust.
Cache and CDN behavior is validated.
Connection, thread, worker, and resource pools are sized and monitored.
Memory, CPU, connection, file-descriptor, storage, and resource leaks are investigated.
Long-running and resource-intensive requests have limits.
Performance is tested with realistic authentication, authorization, data volume, cache state, devices, and networks.
Client telemetry does not materially harm performance.
Performance objectives connect to user and business outcomes.
Forecast data, file, index, queue, log, telemetry, and backup growth.
Identify the maximum safe capacity of every critical component.
Load tests use realistic request mixes, authorization, data distributions, and dependency behavior.
Provider quotas, account limits, concurrency limits, and regional limits are reviewed.
Database connections, locks, storage, replicas, and input/output have sufficient headroom.
Queue, cache, load-balancer, network, worker, and telemetry systems have sufficient headroom.
Scaling does not overload databases or dependencies.
Capacity remains sufficient during the failures the architecture promises to survive.
Rate limits and per-user or per-tenant quotas protect shared capacity fairly.
Retry storms and thundering-herd behavior are prevented.
DDoS and volumetric-abuse scenarios are reviewed.
Capacity alerts provide enough time to act.
Expected and peak operational cost are modeled.
Cost controls do not silently terminate essential operation.
SLOs cover important availability, latency, correctness, durability, freshness, and quality outcomes.
Product and engineering stakeholders approve the SLOs.
Critical dependency reliability is compatible with the product SLO or engineered around.
Retries are bounded, delayed, jittered where appropriate, and safe or idempotent.
Bulkheads or equivalent isolation prevent one workload from exhausting all capacity.
Optional functionality failure does not unnecessarily fail the whole product.
Instances stop receiving new work before shutdown.
In-flight work is completed, transferred, canceled safely, or retried during shutdown.
Shared control planes, identity systems, networks, storage, DNS, providers, and dependencies are included in failure analysis.
Network delay, packet loss, partition, and DNS failure have been tested.
Dependency timeout, malformed response, throttling, partial failure, and outage have been tested.
Database failover, replication lag, and split-brain prevention have been tested.
Disk-full, memory pressure, CPU exhaustion, file-descriptor exhaustion, connection exhaustion, and quota exhaustion have been tested.
Clock skew, time-service failure, certificate expiry, and key expiry have been considered.
Scheduled jobs handle overlapping and missed execution.
Controlled fault injection or equivalent resilience tests are completed for high-risk paths.
Recovery time from tested failures meets approved objectives.
Identify the system of interest, environment, stakeholders, concerns, boundaries, assumptions, and lifecycle stage.
Use viewpoints and models suited to each stakeholder concern rather than one overloaded diagram.
Describe structure, behavior, data, deployment, trust, operations, failure, and evolution where material.
Maintain consistency among architecture descriptions, source, infrastructure, configuration, data flows, and deployment reality.
Record material decisions with context, options, forces, evidence, trade-offs, consequences, owner, status, and revisit triggers.
Separate architecture constraints from temporary implementation choices.
Define architectural invariants and verify them automatically where practical.
Assess quality-attribute trade-offs explicitly instead of optimizing one dimension in isolation.
Use prototypes, models, benchmarks, and experiments to reduce high-impact uncertainty.
Review architecture before irreversible commitment and after material change.
Measure architecture conformance without freezing legitimate evolution.
Document intentional violations and migration plans.
Retire superseded decisions while preserving history and rationale.
Make architecture understandable to implementers, operators, security reviewers, product owners, and maintainers.
Treat architecture as a continuous decision process, not a one-time phase or document.
Partition the system around cohesive responsibilities and change drivers.
Give each module a clear purpose, owner, public contract, and prohibited dependencies.
Keep internal representation and implementation details hidden behind stable boundaries.
Minimize knowledge of remote internals, shared mutable state, temporal order, deployment topology, and incidental data shape.
Prefer explicit dependencies over ambient globals, service locators, hidden context, or action at a distance.
Direct dependencies toward more stable policies and abstractions where this reduces change propagation.
Avoid cyclic dependencies or contain and document them when temporarily unavoidable.
Use dependency graphs and change-impact evidence to identify excessive coupling.
Ensure modules can be tested in isolation with realistic contracts.
Prevent shared utility modules from becoming unowned dumping grounds.
Keep boundary crossings observable and failure-aware.
Align consistency, authorization, privacy, and ownership boundaries intentionally.
Do not split components solely to imitate a fashionable architecture or maximize service count.
Do not combine unrelated responsibilities solely to avoid interface design.
Refactor boundaries when recurring changes, incidents, or coordination costs show the current partition is wrong.
Give each unit one coherent reason to change at its chosen level of abstraction.
Separate policies that change for different stakeholders, rates, or reasons.
Prefer extension through stable composition or explicit variation points when recurring change is evidenced.
Do not introduce speculative extension mechanisms without a credible variation need.
Ensure replacements preserve all required preconditions, postconditions, invariants, side effects, error semantics, timing, and security properties.
Do not strengthen accepted inputs or weaken promised outputs in substitutes.
Keep interfaces focused on cohesive client needs rather than provider convenience.
Prevent clients from depending on operations or data they do not use.
Depend on stable contracts at policy boundaries when doing so reduces volatility and improves testability.
Keep dependency inversion from degenerating into unnecessary wrappers over stable trivial behavior.
Make ownership and lifetime of injected dependencies explicit.
Test contract conformance across implementations and substitutes.
Review SOLID choices together with simplicity, performance, locality, and cognitive load.
Use composition over inheritance when inheritance does not represent a true substitutable relationship.
Refactor violations when they cause change amplification, fragile tests, unsafe substitution, or duplicated policy.
Eliminate duplicated authoritative knowledge that can diverge, not merely visually similar code.
Keep one clear source of truth for rules, schemas, constants, permissions, and state transitions where practical.
Allow local duplication when premature unification would couple unrelated change drivers.
Prefer the simplest design that satisfies current requirements, quality attributes, and credible near-term evolution.
Measure simplicity by ease of understanding, change, testing, operation, and failure recovery—not line count alone.
Avoid frameworks, layers, services, abstractions, configuration, and indirection without demonstrated benefit.
Do not implement optionality, scale, integrations, or policies unsupported by an evidenced requirement.
Preserve reversible seams around high-uncertainty decisions without building the unused future behind them.
Remove dead code, stale flags, unused fields, obsolete interfaces, and abandoned compatibility paths.
Choose the least powerful language, data format, permission, and mechanism that safely solves the problem.
Make ordinary paths obvious and exceptional paths explicit.
Prefer boring, understood technology for undifferentiated problems unless evidence justifies novelty.
Reevaluate abstractions after the third real variation rather than applying a mechanical occurrence count.
Document intentional duplication or complexity where trade-offs make it safer.
Treat cognitive load and operational burden as first-class costs in design review.
Reuse stable knowledge and capabilities only when consumers share genuinely compatible semantics and quality needs.
Define the reusable asset's scope, supported contexts, assumptions, constraints, ownership, and service level.
Separate common core behavior from explicit, bounded variation points.
Avoid configuration that permits invalid or untested combinations.
Design contracts for consumers rather than exposing provider internals.
Version reusable assets and publish compatibility, deprecation, and migration policy.
Test every supported variant and representative combinations.
Provide reference examples, integration tests, and failure semantics.
Track consumers so security fixes and breaking changes can be coordinated.
Avoid copy-and-paste forks that lose provenance and maintenance unless isolation is an intentional trade-off.
Avoid central shared platforms that become mandatory bottlenecks without consumer governance.
Measure reuse by reduced total lifecycle cost and consistent quality, not raw adoption count.
Allow teams to leave a shared asset through documented interfaces and data portability.
Fund maintenance, support, security, documentation, and evolution of shared assets.
Retire variants and consumers that no longer justify their complexity.
Identify every stateful element and assign an authoritative owner.
Distinguish domain state, session state, presentation state, configuration, cache, derived state, and transient workflow state.
Define state schema, invariants, legal transitions, initiating actors, guards, side effects, and terminal states.
Maintain one authoritative source for each fact and make replicas or projections explicitly derived.
Prevent impossible, ambiguous, partially committed, or silently divergent state.
Define consistency, durability, freshness, ordering, and conflict-resolution requirements per state.
Make transitions atomic where partial effects are unacceptable.
Use idempotency, versioning, compare-and-set, or equivalent controls for repeated and concurrent updates.
Define initialization, hydration, synchronization, invalidation, expiry, persistence, migration, and reset behavior.
Preserve user work across retries, navigation, process restart, failover, and offline recovery where required.
Avoid hidden mutable global state and uncontrolled two-way synchronization.
Ensure authorization and tenant context are part of security-sensitive state decisions.
Make state changes auditable and diagnosable without exposing sensitive values.
Test transition coverage, illegal transitions, races, stale reads, duplicate events, and recovery.
Provide repair and reconciliation for state divergence that cannot be eliminated.
Identify shared resources, concurrent actors, ordering dependencies, contention points, and critical invariants.
State the required consistency and isolation semantics rather than relying on platform defaults.
Keep transaction boundaries aligned with business invariants.
Minimize transaction duration and avoid interactive or external work inside locks where possible.
Prevent lost updates, dirty reads, nonrepeatable decisions, duplicate effects, overselling, double spending, and stale authorization.
Use optimistic or pessimistic control deliberately based on conflict rate and failure cost.
Make retried operations idempotent or detect duplicate execution.
Define ordering and conflict-resolution behavior for asynchronous and replicated updates.
Avoid distributed transactions unless their guarantees and failure modes are required and understood.
Use sagas or compensating actions only when compensation semantics are valid and observable.
Prevent deadlock, livelock, starvation, priority inversion, and unbounded contention.
Bound queues, locks, semaphores, pools, and parallelism.
Propagate cancellation, deadlines, and backpressure across concurrent work.
Test with deterministic scheduling, stress, race detection, fault injection, and invariant checking as appropriate.
Reconcile and repair after partial failure without concealing lost or duplicated work.
Treat every remote call as fallible, delayed, duplicated, reordered, throttled, or unavailable.
Define timeouts, deadlines, retry eligibility, backoff, jitter, circuit breaking, and fallback per dependency.
Prevent retry amplification across layers.
Define message delivery, ordering, partitioning, retention, replay, and deduplication semantics.
Make consumers idempotent when duplicate delivery is possible.
Use immutable event facts and version schemas compatibly.
Do not expose internal database change as a public event contract without an intentional compatibility layer.
Use outbox, inbox, transactional messaging, or reconciliation where state and event consistency matters.
Bound queues and define overload, dead-letter, poison-message, and replay behavior.
Preserve tenant, identity, trace, privacy, and authorization context across asynchronous boundaries.
Make causality and correlation observable without assuming a single global clock.
Design for network partitions and independent service evolution.
Avoid synchronous dependency chains that create fragile availability coupling.
Test partial failure, stale replicas, clock skew, split-brain, failover, rebalancing, and consumer lag.
Provide reconciliation capable of detecting missing, duplicated, delayed, or contradictory effects.
Design interfaces from consumer tasks and domain contracts rather than internal storage models.
Define ownership, intended consumers, trust level, availability, latency, consistency, and support expectations.
Use explicit schemas for requests, responses, events, errors, and compatibility rules.
Choose synchronous, asynchronous, batch, stream, or file integration according to semantics and failure tolerance.
Keep transport concerns separate from domain behavior where practical.
Make authentication, authorization, tenant, privacy, and data-classification requirements part of the contract.
Use stable identifiers and avoid leaking implementation-specific keys without need.
Define pagination, filtering, sorting, concurrency, idempotency, rate, quota, and bulk semantics.
Use consistent error taxonomy and distinguish retryable, terminal, conflict, validation, authorization, and dependency failures.
Avoid chatty interfaces and cyclic service dependencies.
Support independent deployment through consumer-driven contracts and compatible evolution.
Define deprecation, discovery, change notification, migration, and retirement.
Make external calls observable and attributable to user and business journeys.
Provide reconciliation for integrations that can lose or duplicate effects.
Evaluate whether an interface should exist before creating another permanent compatibility obligation.
Identify expected change dimensions and isolate the most volatile policies from stable mechanisms.
Prefer reversible decisions where uncertainty is high.
Make schemas, protocols, configuration, data, and deployment capable of compatible staged evolution.
Design migrations before introducing states that cannot be changed safely.
Track technical debt as a specific obligation with cause, consequence, interest, owner, and remediation trigger.
Distinguish deliberate short-term debt from accidental complexity, defects, missing controls, and obsolete technology.
Do not use technical debt as a label to hide security, privacy, accessibility, or reliability nonconformance.
Measure change lead time, regression rate, dependency impact, coordination cost, and operational burden.
Use automated architecture and compatibility checks for critical invariants.
Keep replacement seams around volatile external providers and end-of-life components.
Remove compatibility layers after consumers migrate.
Reserve capacity for modernization and debt reduction based on evidence of risk and cost.
Validate that refactoring changes structure without silently changing behavior.
Use strangler, parallel run, shadowing, dual read/write, or other migration patterns only with reconciliation and exit criteria.
Review whether the architecture still fits scale, team topology, risk, and product strategy.
Define supported environments, clients, protocols, formats, versions, locales, and integration partners.
Use open, stable, documented standards when they satisfy requirements.
Document intentional proprietary dependencies and the value that justifies them.
Separate domain data and policy from provider-specific control planes where practical.
Maintain export and import paths for data, configuration, identities, and audit history where continuity requires them.
Define backward, forward, source, binary, schema, behavioral, and operational compatibility as applicable.
Test mixed-version operation and rolling upgrades where versions coexist.
Use capability negotiation rather than unreliable version inference when appropriate.
Avoid undocumented behavior and implementation quirks as required contracts.
Preserve semantic meaning across serialization, precision, time zones, encodings, and locales.
Make migration tooling resumable, observable, reversible or safely roll-forward, and reconcilable.
Validate backups and recovery in the intended alternate environment where portability is a continuity control.
Track end-of-support dates for platforms and protocols.
Do not promise portability that has never been tested.
Review lock-in at major procurement and architecture decisions, including exit cost and time.
Define sustainability objectives alongside performance, reliability, cost, and user outcomes.
Measure energy, carbon, compute, memory, storage, network transfer, and hardware utilization where material.
Use a transparent measurement boundary, time period, allocation method, data source, and uncertainty statement.
Reduce unnecessary computation, polling, transfer, storage, duplication, and retention.
Prefer efficient algorithms and data structures where end-to-end impact is material.
Scale resources to actual demand without degrading required resilience or latency.
Use batching, caching, compression, scheduling, and locality only when correctness and freshness remain satisfied.
Extend useful system and device lifetime by avoiding needless client requirements and upgrade pressure.
Consider embodied impact and hardware turnover, not only runtime energy.
Choose regions, schedules, and providers with environmental impact in mind where business and resilience constraints permit.
Avoid shifting emissions or cost to users, suppliers, or other lifecycle stages without accounting for it.
Make measurement and optimization privacy-preserving.
Prevent efficiency targets from reducing accessibility, security, reliability, or user control.
Include environmental requirements in supplier and architecture decisions.
Review regressions and publish internally auditable progress against baselines.
